evidence.text:
Sieben Positionen, die in jedem Wärmepumpen-Angebot stehen müssen.

Vergleiche Angebote nie nur über die Endsumme. Ein günstiges Angebot, in dem drei Positionen fehlen, ist am Ende das teuerste — weil genau diese Punkte später als Nachtrag kommen.

1. Wärmepumpe: Hersteller,
evidence.text_en: Seven positions that must be in every heat pump quote. Never compare quotes by final sum alone. A cheap quote missing three items is ultimately the most expensive one—because exactly these points come later as an extra charge. 1. Heat pump: Manufacturer, model, power in kW, refrigerant. 2. Storage: Buffer and hot water with liter specification, not just 'storage'. 3. Hydraulics and installation: Connection, circulation pumps, fittings, insulation. 4. Electrical installation: Supply line, fuse protection, possibly meter location. 5. Commissioning: Adjustment and hydraulic balancing - not optional. 6. Old system: Dismantling and disposal, with oil including tank. 7. Subsidy processing: Who files the applications, what documentation does the company provide? Point 5 is most frequently left out. A heat pump without hydraulic balancing works, but it runs expensively—and the difference lands on your electricity bill every month. Save this for your next quote discussion.

evidence.text: Wenn du von einer Öl oder Gasheizung kommst, müssen in der Regel größere Heizkörper montiert werden. Damit die Energieeinsparung funktioniert, dürfen die Vorlauftemperaturen nicht zu hoch sein. Bei 60° Vorlauf erreicht du bei 5° Außentemperatur keinen SCOP von 4,77 mehr.
evidence.text_en: If you come from an oil or gas heating system, larger radiators usually need to be installed. For energy savings to work, flow temperatures must not be too high. At 60° flow temperature you won't achieve a SCOP of 4.77 at 5° outside temperature.

evidence.text_en: Hi [name], I can well understand your experience. I'm a real estate agent and frequently see this problem in older buildings. 60°C flow temperature is definitely too high for efficient heat pump use. Ideally 35-45°C. The problem usually lies in the insufficient heating surface of old radiators. They are designed for high flow temperatures, but a heat pump works best with low temperatures. You have two sensible options: 1. Larger/additional radiators – relatively inexpensive effort, can be done immediately. 2. Radiant heating (underfloor/wall) – more expensive but the best long-term solution. For older buildings I would start with larger radiators. Look for low-temperature radiators with more heating surface. That often already brings noticeable improvement without a major construction project.

evidence.text_en:
Dear [name],

as the others have already said, the problem lies with the radiators being too small. This is a typical issue in older building renovations.

I would recommend you consult an energy consultant first. They can calculate what heating load is really needed and whether the existing radiators are sufficient. Often heat pump planning is calculated too superficially.

A retrofit underfloor heating is feasible, but expensive. An alternative could be wall heating in the main rooms. This is less invasive than complete underfloor heating and still provides the desired surface effect for low flow temperatures.

evidence.text_en:
stupid question: I've had my heat pump for a few months and it runs great but now I read that you can save about 100 euros on network fees via §14a. But that apparently only applies to heat pumps with a power consumption of over 4.2 kW. Mine only has a power consumption of about 2.5 kW (5 kW heating output). But I do have an immersion heater that is practically never used. If you included this immersion heater you would be over the 4.2 kW.

Anyway, my installer didn't register the system with the network operator because of its small size and didn't build in an external shutdown device either. Now I'm wondering if I should retrofit this afterwards. Basically the network operator could throttle my heat pump to 4.2 kW but that would have no real effect on my system.

Does anyone have a similar "small" setup? Do you use §14a to save on network fees and how high are the savings from it anyway?

Thanks and best regards

Hello to the group,
I registered because I'm planning to replace a 33-year-old 22 kW gas heating system in an old terraced middle house in Thuringia. The topic is coming at me right now and the current funding is quite interesting. I have a first quote, with a hot water heat pump the whole thing should cost around 45k€ (before funding). Underfloor heating isn't really an option for me, I have radiators. Whether they're large enough remains to be seen. In addition to the gas heating, about 4 cubic meters of wood also goes through the stove in the living room, which actually brings the cozy warmth; gas consumption is about 11,000 kWh per year. The gas heating essentially runs on idle.

The current quote includes a 9 kW pump while keeping the existing radiators. The goal should be to set up conditions so I can submit the subsidy application before the first reduction of the climate speed bonus in early February 27.

I hope I find the necessary information here and look forward to expert input.

evidence.text_en: "55 °C flow temperature? That's where no heat pump works." 🤔 Then let's look at the numbers instead. Before: 🛢️ 2,500 litres heating oil × 1.25 € = 3,125 € Now an air-source heat pump runs here. Check heating surfaces. Know system temperatures. First calculate. Then decide.
